item.research_question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?
item.processing_route: Condition (1): Cast, hot isostatically pressed (HIPed) at 1200 °C for 2 h, homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h, slow cooled at 10 °C/min. Condition (2): Condition (1) solutionized at 1400 °C for 20 min, water quenched. Condition (3): Condition (2) annealed at 600 °C for 120 hrs, water quenched.
item.test_conditions: Room temperature (25 °C) and elevated temperature (600 °C) uniaxial compression tests at an initial strain rate of 0.001 s⁻¹.
key_findings: Condition (1) exhibited a continuous ordered B2 matrix with discrete BCC precipitates, resulting in a yield strength of 2032 MPa but only 4.7% compressive fracture strain.
Condition (2) formed a single-phase weakly ordered BCC structure with nanometer-scale B2 regions, achieving >60% compressive ductility but a lower yield strength of 1065 MPa.

Condition (3) achieved an 'inverted' microstructure with a continuous disordered BCC matrix and discrete ~50 nm B2 precipitates, yielding 1345 MPa and 38% compressive fracture strain at room temperature.
Condition (3) showed anomalous strengthening at 600 °C with a yield strength of 1423 MPa (higher than at room temperature) and 16.2% fracture strain.
The hardness values were 562 ± 16 HV for Condition (1), 405 ± 11 HV for Condition (2), and 475 ± 12 HV for Condition (3).
APT analysis revealed strong elemental partitioning: B2 phases were rich in Al and Zr, while BCC phases were rich in Nb and Ta.
The continuous B2 matrix in Condition (1) was identified as the cause of brittleness, whereas the continuous BCC matrix in Condition (3) enabled significant ductility.
item.mechanism: The authors attribute the poor ductility of Condition (1) to the continuous ordered B2 matrix, which is inherently brittle. The improved ductility in Condition (3) is achieved by 'inverting' the microstructure so that the ductile, disordered BCC phase forms the continuous matrix, allowing for dislocation mobility, while the hard B2 phase provides precipitation strengthening. The anomalous strengthening at 600 °C in Condition (3) is speculated to result from competing slip systems in the complex B2 phase (e.g., <001>{110} and <111>{112}) leading to sessile kinks or dislocation debris, though this is not confirmed.
item.limitations: The study does not quantify the specific parameters required for classical precipitation hardening models (e.g., lattice misfit, elastic properties, interfacial energies) due to the complexity of the RHEA. The mechanism for anomalous strengthening at 600 °C is highly speculative and not experimentally verified within this work.
item.future_work: The authors recommend additional scientific studies to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions on precipitation strengthening parameters, further investigation of deformation mechanisms at room temperature and 600 °C, and studies at higher temperatures and under tensile loading.
quotes: This paper presents a novel approach to microstructural engineering of RHEAs to form an 'inverted' BCC + B2 microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates dispersed within a continuous BCC matrix
The brittle nature of Condition (1) is due to the presence of continuous B2 channels, whereas Condition (2) is largely a single-phase BCC alloy with a small degree compositional fluctuations
The ductility of this alloy was substantially increased via microstructural engineering involving controlled annealing treatments, resulting in a phase inversion
